deep.reconstruction:
The page continues the previous folio. It is a set of index (discrete-logarithm) tables in the Gaussian integers Z[i], one for each prime modulus π (or the prime 3), listed in decreasing norm D = N(π) = 37, 29, 17, 13, 9, 5. Each block has the same two parts.

(a) 'Potenzen der Primitiv-Wurzel'. A generator g of (Z[i]/π)^* is chosen, and g^k mod π is listed for k = 0..(D-1)/4. The last entry is always +i. Since ind(i) = (D-1)/4, every residue is i^q·g^r, so this short list of powers determines the whole cyclic group of order D-1.

(b) 'Indices der Elementargrößen'. This gives ind_g(x) mod D-1 for a fixed list of small 'elementary' Gaussian numbers: the unit i, then 1+i and 1-i, then the primes a+bi with a ≡ 1 mod 4 and b even: 1±2i, -3, -3±2i, 1±4i, 5±2i, 1±6i (5±4i, -7, ... on the previous page). The purpose (my inference, near certain) is computing biquadratic residue characters, [x/π]_4 = i^{ind(x)}, for example to test biquadratic reciprocity and the supplementary laws for i and 1+i.

Verification method (mine). For a prime π of norm p, Z[i]/π ≅ F_p via i ↦ r with r^2 ≡ -1 mod p and π ≡ 0.

1. π = 1+6i, p = 37: i ↦ 6, g = -1+i ↦ 5, a primitive root mod 37.
 - Powers: g^2 = -2i, g^3 = 2+2i, g^4 ≡ -4 ≡ 2-i, g^5 ≡ -1+3i, g^6 ≡ -1+2i, g^8 ≡ -2+3i, g^9 ≡ i.
 - g^7 = (-1+2i)(-1+i) = -1-3i ≡ +3i. The page reads -3i.
 - Indices: i 9, 1+i 28, 1-i 19, 1+2i 13, 1-2i 24, -3+2i 32, -3-2i 17, 1+4i 2, 1-4i 3, 5+2i 5, 5-2i 10, 1-6i 11.
 - -3 is given index 34; the correct value is 16 (g^16 = 256 ≡ -3), and 34 is the index of +3.

2. π = 5+2i, p = 29: i ↦ 12, g = -1+i ↦ 11, primitive.
 - Powers: -2i, 2+2i, 1+2i, 2+i, -3+i, i (k = 2..7).
 - Indices: i 7, 1+i 22, 1-i 15, 1+2i 4, 1-2i 26, -3 3, -3+2i 13, -3-2i 9, 1+4i 20, 1-4i 1 (indeed 1-4i ≡ g), 5-2i 11.
 - All correct.

3. π = 1+4i, p = 17: i ↦ 4, g = 1-2i ↦ 10, primitive.
 - Powers: g^2 ≡ -2, g^3 ≡ 1-i, g^4 ≡ i.
 - Indices: i 4, 1+i 7, 1-i 3, 1+2i 6, 1-2i 1, -3 3 (since -3 ≡ 1-i mod 1+4i), -3+2i 7, -3-2i 5, 1-4i 10.
 - All correct.

4. π = -3+2i, p = 13: i ↦ 8, g = 1-i ↦ 6, primitive. Here it is called 'Elementar-Wurzel'.
 - Powers: g^2 = -2i, g^3 ≡ i.
 - Indices: i 3, 1+i 4, 1-i 1, 1+2i 10, 1-2i 11, -3 2, -3-2i 7.
 - All correct. With modulus +3+2i the root 1-i would have g^3 ≡ 1, not i, so the blotted sign must be minus.

5. Modulus 3 (inert; Z[i]/3 = F_9, D = 9, group order 8): g = 1-i, g^2 = -2i ≡ i.
 - Indices: i 2, 1+i 3 (= i·g), 1+2i ≡ 1-i gives 1, 1-2i ≡ 1+i gives 3.
 - Correct.

6. π = 1+2i, p = 5: i ↦ 2, root i.
 - Indices: i 1, 1+i ↦ 3 gives 3, 1-i ↦ 4 gives 2, 1-2i ↦ 2 gives 1.
 - Correct.

So the page is computational groundwork for Gauss's theory of biquadratic residues in Z[i]: discrete logarithms modulo Gaussian primes of small norm.
errors: Modulus 1+6i, power table: entry k=7 is written -3i, but (-1+i)^7 = -8-8i ≡ -1-3i ≡ +3i (mod 1+6i). The neighbouring entries g^6 = -1+2i and g^8 = -2+3i are consistent only with g^7 ≡ +3i, so this is a sign slip (or a misreading of +).

Modulus 1+6i, index table: ind(-3) is given as 34, but (-1+i)^16 = 256 ≡ -3 (mod 1+6i), so ind(-3) = 16. The value 34 = 16+18 is ind(+3), a sign slip in -1. It matters because ind mod 4 = 2 is correct either way, but ind mod 36 is not.
All other entries in all six blocks check out.

results.what: Index (discrete logarithm) tables for primitive roots modulo Gaussian primes 1+6i, 5+2i, 1+4i, -3+2i, 3, 1+2i, giving power tables up to g^{(N-1)/4} = i and indices of a fixed set of small primes and units
results.modern_name: Discrete logarithm / index tables in Z[i] (Gaussian analogue of Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus); multiplicative group of the finite field Z[i]/(π)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (biquadratic residue theory, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum 1828/1832); rational index tables to Jacobi (Canon Arithmeticus, 1839)

results.what: Use of ind(x) mod 4 to read off the biquadratic (quartic) residue character [x/π]_4 = i^{ind x}, including the characters of i and 1+i (supplementary laws), presumably for numerical testing of biquadratic reciprocity
results.modern_name: Quartic residue symbol and quartic reciprocity with its supplementary laws
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (stated 1832); first published proofs by Eisenstein (1844) and Jacobi in lectures

results.what: Compact power table listing only g^0..g^{(N-1)/4} ending at i, since every residue is i^q g^r
results.modern_name: Coset decomposition of the cyclic group modulo the unit subgroup <i>

deep.surprise_reason: Gaussian-integer index tables are exactly the computational groundwork expected for Gauss's well-known theory of biquadratic residues. The material is routine and squarely his; only the specific tables (and two small sign slips) are unpublished detail.

checkable.asserts: Gives -2+I, a Gaussian integer, so (-1+i)^7 ≡ +3i mod 1+6i; the page's -3i is a slip.
Not a Gaussian integer, so (-1+i)^7 is not ≡ -3i mod 1+6i.
Gaussian integer, so g^9 ≡ i mod 1+6i, i.e. ind(i) = 9.
Under i↦6, g↦5 mod 37, the indices for i, 1+i, 1-i, 1+2i, 1-2i, -3+2i, -3-2i, 1+4i, 1-4i, 5+2i, 5-2i, 1-6i agree with the images of these elements.
ind(-3) mod 1+6i is 16, not 34 as written; 34 is ind(+3).

checkable.asserts: The images of the roots -1+i (mod 1+6i and mod 5+2i), 1-2i (mod 1+4i), 1-i (mod -3+2i) and i (mod 1+2i) are primitive roots.
The modulus 5+2i index table is correct under i↦12.
The modulus 1+4i index table is correct under i↦4.
The modulus -3+2i index table is correct under i↦8.
Gives -I, a Gaussian integer, so (1-i)^2 ≡ i mod 3, i.e. ind(i) = 2 in F_9.

Modulus 1+6i: the blotted element with index 19 is +1-i (confirmed).
